blocks.md:
- Explain, in your own words, why a time signature is called 'simple' or 'compound' based on how its beat divides.
- Read and count rhythms in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8, grouping notes and rests correctly.
- Look at any time signature covered so far and state whether it is simple or compound.
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md:
Every piece of music has a steady pulse running through it. That pulse is called the **beat**. You have already worked with beats throughout this course: counting "1, 2, 3, 4" in 4/4, feeling the strong first beat in a bar of 3/4, and so on.

Now we are going to look a little more closely at what is happening *inside* each beat.

**The beat divides** means: each beat can be split into smaller, equal pieces. The number of pieces each beat splits into is one of the most important ideas in music theory, and it is the whole reason we have two families of time signature: **simple time** and **compound time**.

Think of the beat like a slice of cake. You can cut each slice into two equal pieces, or into three equal pieces. The cake is still the same size. But the feeling you get is very different depending on which cut you make. Music works the same way.

blocks.text: A Clapping Exercise: Hear the Difference First

blocks.md: Before we look at any notation, try this quick exercise with your hands.

Clap once per second, very evenly. Count out loud: "1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4..."

Keep going for about eight beats. This is your pulse. Every other clap in this exercise will fit inside this steady beat.
blocks.title: Step 1: Clap a steady beat

blocks.label: Listen: a steady beat, four beats

blocks.md:
Now clap twice inside every beat, evenly spaced. Each pair of claps must fit neatly into one beat before the next beat arrives.

Count out loud: "1-and, 2-and, 3-and, 4-and..."

The word "and" lands exactly halfway through the beat. This two-in-a-beat feel is what we call **simple time**.
blocks.title: Step 2: Split each beat into TWO (simple)

blocks.label: Listen: beat divided into two (simple feel, 4 beats)

blocks.md:
Now try to fit THREE claps inside every beat, all evenly spaced.

Count out loud: "1-and-a, 2-and-a, 3-and-a, 4-and-a..."

It produces a gentle, rolling, slightly "lilting" feeling. This three-in-a-beat feel is what we call **compound time**.

Do this a few times back to back: two claps per beat, then three claps per beat. Notice how different they feel, even though the main beat stays the same speed.
blocks.title: Step 3: Split each beat into THREE (compound)

blocks.label: Listen: beat divided into three (compound feel, 4 beats)

blocks.md: Those two sounds, two-in-a-beat and three-in-a-beat, are the heart of this whole lesson. Everything else, the time signatures, the notation, the counting, is just a way of writing down which one a piece of music is using.

If the three-in-a-beat clapping feels awkward, try thinking of a familiar word with three syllables, like "strawberry" or "elephant". Say it in time with the beat: "STRAW-ber-ry, STRAW-ber-ry..." Each syllable is one of the three equal divisions. That rolling, triplet-like feel is compound time.

Away from the piano, set a timer for 30 seconds. Tap a steady beat with your foot. At the same time, clap twice per beat for 15 seconds, counting "1-and" aloud. Then switch to three claps per beat for 15 seconds, counting "1-and-a" aloud. Notice the difference in feel. You do not need to play anything yet, just get comfortable with the two sensations.

items.prompt: What does it mean when we say 'the beat divides'?
items.explain: The beat divides means that each beat can be split into smaller equal parts. How many parts it splits into is what defines simple and compound time.
options: The music gets quieter on every other beat.
Each beat can be split into smaller, equal parts.
The bar line divides the music into equal sections.
The tempo speeds up and then slows down.

items.prompt: When you clap three times inside every beat, counting '1-and-a', which family of time does that represent?
items.explain: Compound time is defined by each beat dividing into three equal parts. Clapping '1-and-a' puts three equal claps inside every beat, which is exactly that compound feel.
options: Simple time, because there are three beats in the bar.
Compound time, because each beat divides into three equal parts.
Simple time, because three is an odd number.
Compound time, because the tempo is faster.

items.prompt: In both simple time and compound time, the main steady beat stays the same. The only difference is how many equal parts each beat is divided into.
items.explain: Correct. The beat itself is unchanged. Simple time divides each beat into two equal parts, and compound time divides each beat into three equal parts. That difference in division is what sets them apart.

blocks.text: Simple Time Revisited: The Beat Splits in Two

blocks.md: Before we look at anything new, let's pin down exactly what **simple time** means. The word "simple" here does not mean "easy". It means something very specific about how each beat behaves.
**Simple time** is any time signature in which every beat divides naturally into **two equal halves**. That is the whole definition. If the beat splits into two, the time is simple.

You already know 4/4 well, so let's use it as the example. In 4/4, the beat is a **quarter note (crotchet)**. One quarter note lasts for one beat. If you cut that beat exactly in half, you get two **eighth notes**. Two eighth notes fit perfectly inside one quarter note beat. That is the split in action.

blocks.caption: Left bar: one quarter note (one beat). Right bar: two eighth notes (the same beat split in two). Each bar lasts exactly one beat.

blocks.md: Now let's make it musical. Here is the bottom part of a C major scale, played first with one quarter note per note (the beat), then again with each note split into two eighth notes. The metronome click stays on the beat throughout, so you can hear exactly how the eighth notes sit inside it.

blocks.label: C major scale fragment: one quarter note per note (the beat)
Same scale fragment: each note played twice as eighth notes, splitting each beat in two

blocks.md: Sit at the piano and find C4 (middle C). Set a slow, steady pulse by tapping your foot or counting aloud: one, two, three, four. Now play C4 twice for each foot-tap, keeping both notes even. Move up: D, E, F, G, doing the same. You are playing eighth notes against a quarter note beat. Notice how two eighth notes fill one beat exactly.

blocks.label: The notes used in the scale fragment: C D E F G

blocks.text: All the Time Signatures You Already Know Are Simple

blocks.md: Look at every time signature you have studied so far. Every single one is a simple time signature. Here they are together:

In each of these, the **top number** tells you how many beats there are in a bar. The **bottom number** tells you what kind of note gets one beat. And in every case, that beat note splits naturally into **two equal halves**. That is what makes them all simple.

- **2/4**: 2 beats per bar, each beat is a quarter note. One quarter note splits into 2 eighth notes. Simple.
- **3/4**: 3 beats per bar, each beat is a quarter note. One quarter note splits into 2 eighth notes. Simple.
- **4/4**: 4 beats per bar, each beat is a quarter note. One quarter note splits into 2 eighth notes. Simple.
- **2/2**: 2 beats per bar, each beat is a half note (minim). One half note splits into 2 quarter notes. Simple.
- **3/2**: 3 beats per bar, each beat is a half note. One half note splits into 2 quarter notes. Simple.
- **4/2**: 4 beats per bar, each beat is a half note. One half note splits into 2 quarter notes. Simple.
- **3/8**: 3 beats per bar, each beat is an eighth note (quaver). One eighth note splits into 2 sixteenth notes. Simple.
blocks.title: Why each one is simple

blocks.md: A quick way to spot simple time: look at the top number of the time signature. If it is **2, 3, or 4**, the time signature is almost certainly simple. Those numbers count the beats directly, and simple-time beats always split into two.

You might wonder: what if the beat splits into **three** instead of two? That is exactly the question the next section answers. A time signature where every beat splits into three equal parts is called **compound time**, and it looks quite different on the page.

items.prompt: In simple time, each beat divides into how many equal parts?
items.explain: Simple time means every beat splits into exactly two equal halves. That is the defining feature of simple time.

items.prompt: In 4/4, one quarter note beat splits into two equal halves. What are those two halves called?
items.explain: A quarter note split in half gives two eighth notes. Two eighth notes equal exactly one quarter note in length.

items.prompt: 3/8 is a simple time signature because its beat (an eighth note) divides into two equal sixteenth notes.
items.explain: Correct. In 3/8, each beat is an eighth note. An eighth note divides into two sixteenth notes, so the beat splits into two. That makes 3/8 a simple time signature.

blocks.text: Compound Time: The Beat Splits in Three

blocks.md:
In the last section you saw that simple time slices every beat into two equal halves. Now for the other main family: **compound time**.

In compound time, every beat divides into exactly **three** equal parts, not two. That triple split is the one defining feature of compound time. Everything else follows from it.
**Compound time:** a time signature in which every beat divides naturally into three equal parts.

Three-part beats produce a very distinctive sound. Instead of a straight, even pulse, the music develops a gentle rolling quality, sometimes described as a **lilt**. Think of a lullaby, a boat rocking on water, or an Irish jig. That swaying, forward-leaning feeling almost always comes from beats that split into three.

Before looking at any notation, just listen. The clip below plays four notes on middle C. Each note lasts one beat, and each beat is divided into three equal mini-pulses underneath. Count along quietly: **one-and-a, two-and-a, three-and-a, four-and-a**. Notice how the counting rocks forward with a slight lean on the first of each group of three.

blocks.label: Four notes, each beat divided into three: one-and-a, two-and-a, three-and-a, four-and-a

blocks.md: Now hear the same four notes shaped into a simple lilting melody. The beat still splits into three throughout.

blocks.label: A short lilting melody in compound feel: each beat divides into three

blocks.md:
Place your right hand in C major position (thumb on C4). Play these five notes slowly and evenly: C, D, E, F, G.

1. First, count **one-and, two-and, three-and, four-and, five-and** as you play, dividing each note into two. Keep it perfectly straight and even.
2. Then play the same five notes and count **one-and-a, two-and-a, three-and-a, four-and-a, five-and-a**, pushing the 'and' forward so the three mini-pulses roll together. Let your wrist relax and follow the natural sway.

The second version should feel looser and more lilting. That rolling sway is compound time.

blocks.label: Play these five notes and feel the difference between a two-split and a three-split on each one

blocks.md: A helpful image: simple time feels like walking, steady and even, left-right-left-right. Compound time feels like skipping, where one step is longer and the next is shorter, giving a one-two-three lurch that pulls you forward. Both are perfectly regular. They just divide the beat differently.

items.prompt: In compound time, every beat divides into how many equal parts?
items.explain: Compound time is defined by every beat dividing into exactly three equal parts. That triple subdivision is what gives compound time its characteristic lilting feel.
options: It varies from beat to beat

items.prompt: If you change from a simple feel to a compound feel on the same notes, the pitch of the notes changes.
items.explain: The pitches stay exactly the same. Only the subdivision changes, from two mini-pulses per beat to three. The notes themselves are unaffected.

items.prompt: Think of a song or piece of music you know that feels lilting, rocking, or swaying. Can you hum or tap it now and feel whether the beat seems to divide into three? What is the piece, and how would you describe the feel?

blocks.md: You have already seen time signatures like 4/4 and 3/4, where the beat is a quarter note. Compound time signatures look a little different, but once you know the trick they make perfect sense.

The three main compound time signatures are:
- 6/8
- 9/8
- 12/8

All three share the same bottom number: **8**. That 8 means the written note value is a **eighth note**. The top number then tells you how many of those eighth notes fill one bar.

**The two numbers, explained plainly**

- **Bottom number (8):** the written note value is an eighth note.
- **Top number (6, 9 or 12):** how many eighth notes fit in one bar.

So 6/8 means "six eighth notes per bar", 9/8 means "nine eighth notes per bar", and 12/8 means "twelve eighth notes per bar". You could fill each bar by writing that many eighth notes in a row, and the bar would be exactly full.

L:1/8

blocks.text: Finding the Real Beats: Divide the Top Number by 3

blocks.md: Here is the key insight. In compound time, every beat is a **dotted quarter note**. A dotted quarter note lasts for three eighth notes. So to find how many beats are actually in a bar, you divide the top number by 3.

**The golden rule for compound time signatures:**

Top number divided by 3 = number of dotted-quarter note beats per bar.

- 6 divided by 3 = **2 beats** (6/8)
- 9 divided by 3 = **3 beats** (9/8)
- 12 divided by 3 = **4 beats** (12/8)

| Time signature | Eighth notes per bar | Divide by 3 | Beats per bar | Feel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6/8 | 6 | 6 / 3 | 2 dotted-quarter note beats | Two big beats, each split into three |
| 9/8 | 9 | 9 / 3 | 3 dotted-quarter note beats | Three big beats, each split into three |
| 12/8 | 12 | 12 / 3 | 4 dotted-quarter note beats | Four big beats, each split into three |
blocks.title: Compound time signatures at a glance

blocks.md: Think of each dotted-quarter note beat as a little group of three eighth notes that belong together. The bar is not a stream of six, nine, or twelve equal ticks. It is two, three, or four **big beats**, each of which rocks gently into three smaller steps.

Let us start with 6/8 because it is the most common compound time signature. Place your right hand on C, E and G above middle C. You are going to play two bars, using only those three notes, in a steady 6/8 pattern.

Each bar has two dotted-quarter note beats. Each beat fills three eighth notes. So the pattern for one bar is:

- Beat 1: C, E, G (three eighth notes)
- Beat 2: C, E, G (three eighth notes)

Count aloud: **1-and-a, 2-and-a** as you play. The "1" and the "2" are the big dotted-quarter note beats. "And" and "a" are the two smaller eighth notes that complete each group.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
"Beat 1"CEG "Beat 2"CEG | "Beat 1"CEG "Beat 2"CEG |]
blocks.caption: Two bars of 6/8: two dotted-quarter note beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes. Count: 1-and-a, 2-and-a.

blocks.label: Two bars of 6/8: C-E-G, C-E-G, C-E-G, C-E-G (eighth notes). Feel two big beats, each rocking into three.

blocks.md: When you listen, try to feel groups of three rather than counting six separate ticks. If you tap your foot twice per bar (once for each big beat), you have found the dotted-quarter note pulse. That gentle rock of "three inside each beat" is the hallmark of compound time.

In 9/8 there are three dotted-quarter note beats per bar. Each beat still divides into three eighth notes, giving nine eighth notes in total. Try playing one bar on the notes C, D and E, three eighth notes per beat.
Count: **1-and-a, 2-and-a, 3-and-a**. Three big beats, each with three eighth notes inside.

blocks.caption: One bar of 9/8: three dotted-quarter note beats, each filled with three eighth notes.

blocks.label: One bar of 9/8: C-D-E repeated three times (nine eighth notes). Feel three big beats.

blocks.md: In 12/8 there are four dotted-quarter note beats per bar. This is the compound partner of 4/4: four big beats, but each one splits into three instead of two. You may recognise it from slow blues and gospel music.
Try one bar on C, D, E and G, three eighth notes per beat. Count: **1-and-a, 2-and-a, 3-and-a, 4-and-a**.

blocks.caption: One bar of 12/8: four dotted-quarter note beats, each filled with three eighth notes.

blocks.label: One bar of 12/8: four groups of three eighth notes. Feel four big beats.
The notes used in the 12/8 example: C, D, E and G above middle C.

blocks.md: A handy way to remember all three: the top number is always a multiple of 3. If you see a time signature with 6, 9, or 12 on top and 8 on the bottom, you are in compound time, and you can always find the beat count by dividing the top number by 3.

Sit at the piano and try each compound time signature in turn.

1. **6/8:** Play C-E-G, C-E-G in a repeating loop. Tap your foot twice per bar. Say "1-and-a, 2-and-a" aloud.
2. **9/8:** Play C-D-E, C-D-E, C-D-E in a loop. Tap your foot three times per bar.
3. **12/8:** Play C-D-E-G four times slowly in a loop. Tap your foot four times per bar.

For each one, count how many foot-taps per bar. That number is your dotted-quarter note beat count.

items.prompt: In a compound time signature, what does the bottom number 8 tell you?
items.explain: The bottom number names the written note value. 8 means eighth note. The number of beats is found separately by dividing the top number by 3.
options: There are 8 beats in the bar.
The written note value is an eighth note.
The beat is a dotted quarter note.
The music should be played very fast.

items.prompt: How many dotted-quarter note beats are in each bar of 9/8?
items.explain: Divide the top number by 3: 9 divided by 3 = 3. So there are 3 dotted-quarter note beats per bar in 9/8.

items.prompt: 12/8 has four dotted-quarter note beats per bar, making it the compound equivalent of 4/4.
items.explain: 12 divided by 3 = 4, so 12/8 has four dotted-quarter note beats per bar. Just as 4/4 has four quarter note beats that each split in two, 12/8 has four beats that each split into three eighth notes.

blocks.md:
Use the syllables **"1-and-a"** for each beat. The word "1" lands on the beat itself, "and" is the second eighth note, and "a" is the third eighth note. Then the next beat begins on "2", and so on.

Here is how that looks for each time signature:

- **6/8:** two beats per bar: "1-and-a  2-and-a"
- **9/8:** three beats per bar: "1-and-a  2-and-a  3-and-a"
- **12/8:** four beats per bar: "1-and-a  2-and-a  3-and-a  4-and-a"

Say the syllables evenly and at the same speed every time. Each syllable is one eighth note. Tap your foot on "1" and "2" (the beats), and say "and-a" between taps. This builds the feel of compound time in your body before your fingers ever touch the keys.

Six eighth notes in a row fill one bar of 6/8. Count them like this:

| Eighth note: | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Say: | **1** | and | a | **2** | and | a |

Tap your foot on "1" and "2" only. Everything else is a subdivision of those two beats.

M:6/8
L:1/8

C D E F G A |]
blocks.caption: Six eighth notes in 6/8. Count: 1-and-a  2-and-a. Tap your foot on 1 and 2.

blocks.label: Six eighth notes in 6/8, counted 1-and-a 2-and-a

blocks.text: Grouping Rules: How Notes Are Beamed

blocks.md:
In compound time, beaming (the thick lines that join eighth notes together) is used to show the beats clearly. The rule is simple:

**Beam eighth notes in groups of three to match each beat.**

A reader can then see exactly where each beat starts and ends. Never beam across a beat boundary. Each group of three eighth notes belongs to exactly one beat.

**The standard beat note in compound time is the dotted quarter note.** It lasts three eighth notes, so it fills one complete beat on its own. When you see a dotted quarter note, it takes up beats 1, 2, 3 or 4 all by itself, with no extra beaming needed.

You do not have to fill every beat with three separate eighth notes. Within one beat group you can also use:

- A **dotted quarter note** (one note lasting the whole beat)
- A **quarter note plus an eighth note** (the quarter note lasts two eighth notes, the eighth note lasts one)
- Three separate **eighth notes** beamed together

All three options fill exactly three eighth notes worth of time, so they all fit neatly into one beat.

blocks.caption: Bar 1: two dotted quarter notes (one per beat). Bar 2: one dotted quarter note, then a quarter note and an eighth note. Both bars are correct 6/8 groupings.

blocks.md: A quarter note lasts two eighth notes. When you pair a quarter note with an eighth note inside the same beat, the quarter note comes first and the eighth note follows. This is the only way round that works, because the longer note naturally sits at the start of the beat.
Let's look at some rhythm examples and spot what is right and what is wrong. This is one of the most important skills in compound time.
Six eighth notes in a 6/8 bar, beamed as two groups of three. Each group is one beat. This is correct.
blocks.title: Example 1: Correct beaming

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
C D E F G A |]
blocks.caption: Correct: two groups of three eighth notes. Beat 1 = C-D-E, Beat 2 = F-G-A.

blocks.md: All six eighth notes beamed as one group. This hides the beat in the middle of the bar. A reader cannot tell where beat 2 starts. This is incorrect.
blocks.title: Example 2: Incorrect beaming, all six eighth notes joined together

blocks.abc:

M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
(6CDEFGA |]
blocks.caption: Incorrect: all six eighth notes in one beam. The halfway point (where beat 2 begins) is invisible.

blocks.md: Beaming across the midpoint of a 6/8 bar is one of the most common mistakes. Always split your six eighth notes into two groups of three, even if all six notes are the same pitch.
Beat 1 is a dotted quarter note. Beat 2 uses a quarter note plus an eighth note. Both beats last exactly three eighth notes. This is correct.
blocks.title: Example 3: Correct mix of note values

blocks.caption: Correct: dotted quarter note on beat 1 (C lasts 3 eighth notes), then quarter note F plus eighth note A on beat 2.

blocks.label: Dotted quarter note then quarter note-plus-eighth note in 6/8

blocks.md: Beat 2 has an eighth note followed by a quarter note. The longer note comes after the shorter one. This is incorrect: the eighth note crosses into the next beat's territory in a confusing way, and the quarter note overlaps the beat boundary.
blocks.title: Example 4: Incorrect placement of the longer note

blocks.caption: Incorrect: eighth note A then quarter note F on beat 2. The quarter note pushes across beat 2's three-eighth note limit.

blocks.md: Within any beat in compound time, a quarter note must always come before the eighth note, not after it. A quarter note lasts two eighth notes, so if it came second it would cross the beat boundary.

blocks.abc:

M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
C3 D E F | G2 A B2 c |]
blocks.caption: Two bars of 6/8. Bar 1: dotted quarter note C, then three eighth notes D-E-F. Bar 2: quarter note G plus eighth note A, then quarter note B plus eighth note C.

blocks.label: Two bars of 6/8 rhythm melody, count 1-and-a 2-and-a

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and work through these three steps for the two-bar rhythm above.

1. **Say the counts aloud** without clapping: "1-and-a  2-and-a  1-and-a  2-and-a". Do this slowly until it feels natural.
2. **Clap the rhythm** while saying the counts. Clap only where a note falls: on "1" in bar 1 (the dotted quarter note), then on "2-and-a" for bar 1's three eighth notes, and so on. If you are unsure where a note falls, go back to the notation and match each note head to its syllable.
3. **Play the notes on the piano** with your right hand, still counting aloud. Use any comfortable fingering. The goal is to feel the two-beat pulse while your hand plays the smaller subdivisions inside it.

items.prompt: In 6/8, how many main beats do you count per bar, and what syllables do you use for each?
items.explain: 6/8 has two dotted-quarter note beats per bar. Each beat divides into three eighth notes, so you count 1-and-a for the first beat and 2-and-a for the second. Six beats would be counting every eighth note, which loses the sense of the main pulse.

items.prompt: In 6/8, it is correct to beam all six eighth notes in a bar together into one single group.
items.explain: Beaming all six eighth notes together hides the two beats. The rule is to beam eighth notes in groups of three, one group per beat, so the reader can clearly see where beat 1 ends and beat 2 begins.

items.prompt: Within a single beat in compound time, which combination of notes is written correctly?
items.explain: A quarter note (2 eighth notes) followed by an eighth note (1 eighth note) adds up to exactly 3 eighth notes, which fills one beat in compound time. The quarter note must come first because if a quarter note followed an eighth note it would push across the beat boundary into the next beat. Two quarter notes would equal 4 eighth notes (too long), and four eighth notes would also be too long for a single beat.
options: An eighth note followed by a quarter note
A quarter note followed by an eighth note

blocks.text: Dotted Notes, Ties and Rests in Compound Time

blocks.md: You already know that in compound time each beat is a dotted note worth three eighth notes. That single fact shapes every rhythm you will read and write in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8. This section shows you exactly which note values and rest values feel most natural in compound time, and how to write silence without losing track of the beat.

blocks.text: The dotted quarter note: one full beat

blocks.md:
In 6/8, each beat lasts a dotted quarter note (three eighth notes). A dotted quarter note is a quarter note with a small dot beside it. The dot adds half the quarter note's value, so the total is one-and-a-half quarter note beats, which equals exactly three eighth notes.

When you see a dotted quarter note in 6/8, think: **one full beat**. Nothing more to count.

blocks.caption: Two dotted quarter notes fill one bar of 6/8. Each dotted quarter note = one beat.

blocks.label: Two dotted quarter notes in 6/8: one beat each, hear the two-beat feel

blocks.md: **Dotted quarter note = 1 beat in compound time.** Three eighth notes also equal 1 beat. Both are correct ways to fill one beat.

blocks.text: The dotted half note: two full beats

blocks.md:
A dotted half note is a half note with a dot. It lasts six eighth notes, which is two full compound beats. You will see it most often in 9/8 and 12/8, where there is room for it, but it can appear in 6/8 too, filling an entire bar.

Think of it as two dotted quarter notes tied together into one smooth, long note.

blocks.caption: In 9/8: a dotted half note (6 eighth notes = 2 beats) followed by a dotted quarter note (3 eighth notes = 1 beat). Together they fill the bar.

blocks.label: Dotted half note then dotted quarter note in 9/8: hear two beats then one beat

blocks.text: Quarter note plus eighth note: another way to fill one beat

blocks.md:
A quarter note lasts two eighth notes and an eighth note lasts one eighth note. Together they add up to three eighth notes, so a quarter note followed by an eighth note fills one complete compound beat.

This rhythm has a characteristic lilt. It sounds long-short within the beat, which is very common in jigs and many other compound-time tunes.

blocks.caption: A quarter note plus an eighth note in each beat: E (2 eighths) + F (1 eighth) = one beat; G + A = one beat. Together they fill one 6/8 bar.

blocks.label: Quarter note + eighth note pattern, long-short feel within each beat

blocks.md:
**Three ways to fill one compound beat:**
- A dotted quarter note (one note, full beat)
- Three eighth notes (three equal notes)
- Quarter note + eighth note (long-short)

blocks.text: Rests in compound time: keeping the beat clear

blocks.md:
A rest is a moment of silence. In compound time the golden rule is the same as for notes: **each beat must be clearly visible**. You use rests in combinations that match the beat groupings, so a performer can always see where beat 1 and beat 2 fall.

The two rest values you will use most are:
- The **eighth note rest**: lasts one eighth note (one third of a beat in compound time)
- The **quarter note rest**: lasts two eighth notes (two thirds of a beat)

**Avoid writing a single quarter note rest across the boundary between two beats.** That would blur where one beat ends and the next begins. Always group rests so that each beat can be seen separately.

blocks.text: Replacing a dotted-quarter note beat with rests

blocks.md:
When an entire beat is silent, you have a choice. You can write a single dotted quarter note rest, which is the clearest option and the most common in print. Alternatively, you can write a quarter note rest followed by an eighth note rest, which also adds up to three eighth notes and also works correctly.

Below is a worked example. Look at bar 1 versus bar 2.

Both bars are in 6/8. Both have the same silence on beat 2.

**Bar 1** uses a dotted quarter note rest for beat 2. Clean and simple.

**Bar 2** uses a quarter note rest + eighth note rest for beat 2. Also correct, and sometimes easier to read when surrounding rhythms are complex.

Neither is wrong. A dotted quarter note rest is preferred in most published music.
blocks.title: Dotted-quarter note rest versus quarter note rest + eighth note rest

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
C D E z3 | C D E z2 z |]
blocks.caption: Bar 1: dotted quarter note rest (z3) on beat 2. Bar 2: quarter note rest + eighth note rest (z2 z) on beat 2. Both equal one full beat of silence.

blocks.md: **One silent beat in compound time = a dotted quarter note rest.** You can also write it as a quarter note rest + eighth note rest. Both equal three eighth notes of silence.

blocks.md: Here is a four-bar melody in 6/8 in the treble clef. It uses dotted quarter notes, eighth notes grouped in threes, the quarter note-plus-eighth note rhythm, and a dotted quarter note rest. Play it through slowly, counting two beats per bar: 1-and-a, 2-and-a.

E3 G2 A | B3 A2 G | E2 F G2 E | C3 z3 |]

Bar 3: quarter note+eighth note twice. Bar 4: dotted quarter note C, then a full beat of silence (dotted quarter note rest).

blocks.label: Four-bar 6/8 melody: listen before you play
Notes used in the melody: C, E, F, G, A, B

blocks.md: Sit at your piano and play the four-bar melody above. Start slowly, counting aloud: '1-and-a, 2-and-a' for each bar. When bar 4 arrives, let the C ring for its full dotted quarter note, then lift your hand for the silent beat. Play it three times: once slowly, once at a comfortable pace, once a little faster.

items.prompt: In 6/8, a single beat of silence is most clearly written as which rest value?
items.explain: One beat in compound time equals three eighth notes, which is the value of a dotted quarter note. A dotted quarter note rest is therefore the clearest way to show one full silent beat.

items.prompt: A quarter note followed by an eighth note appears on one beat in 6/8. How many eighth notes do they total?
items.explain: A quarter note = 2 eighth notes and an eighth note = 1 eighth note. Together they make 3 eighth notes, which is exactly one compound beat.

items.prompt: In 9/8, a dotted half note fills two full beats.
items.explain: A dotted half note lasts 6 eighth notes. In 9/8 each beat is 3 eighth notes (a dotted quarter note), so 6 eighth notes = 2 beats. This is correct.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: dotted notes, ties and rests in compound time

blocks.text: Simple or Compound? How to Tell at a Glance

blocks.md: You have now seen both types of time. Let's bring it all together into one clear decision rule you can use whenever you pick up a piece of music.

**The one question to ask:** Is the top number of the time signature 2, 3, or 4? Or is it 6, 9, or 12?

- **2, 3, or 4 = Simple time.** The beat is the note shown by the bottom number.
- **6, 9, or 12 = Compound time.** Divide the top number by 3 to find the number of beats per bar. The beat is a dotted note worth three of the bottom-number notes.

| Time signature | Top number | Type | Beats per bar | Beat note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2/4 | 2 | Simple | 2 | Quarter note |
| 3/4 | 3 | Simple | 3 | Quarter note |
| 4/4 | 4 | Simple | 4 | Quarter note |
| 2/2 | 2 | Simple | 2 | Half note |
| 3/8 | 3 | Simple | 3 | Eighth note |
| 6/8 | 6 | Compound | 2 | Dotted quarter |
| 9/8 | 9 | Compound | 3 | Dotted quarter |
| 12/8 | 12 | Compound | 4 | Dotted quarter |

Here are six time signatures written out on a stave. For each one, ask yourself: is the top number 2, 3, or 4 (simple), or 6, 9, or 12 (compound)? Then work out how many beats are in each bar and what note gets the beat.

blocks.md: Pick any piece you are currently learning. Look at its time signature before you play a single note. Ask the one question: is the top number 2, 3, or 4 (simple) or 6, 9, or 12 (compound)? Write down your answer, then count yourself in aloud at the piano before you play.

Sometimes you will hear a piece before you see the score. Listen to the beat. Now listen inside each beat. Does it feel like it splits into **two** equal parts? That points to simple time. Does it feel like it splits into **three** equal parts, giving a gentle rolling or swaying feel? That points to compound time.

If a slow or flowing piece seems to have three little subdivisions rocking along inside every beat, look at the time signature. Chances are you will see a 6, 9, or 12 at the top. Compound time is the natural home of lullabies, barcarolles, and many folk songs precisely because that triple subdivision gives the music its characteristic lilt.

blocks.label: Simple feel: quarter note beats each split into two (like 3/4)
Compound feel: dotted quarter beats each split into three (like 6/8)

blocks.md: Listen to both clips above back to back. The simple version has a steady, even swing. The compound version has a rolling, lilting quality. Training your ear to hear that difference is just as valuable as reading the time signature on the page.

items.prompt: A piece is marked with a time signature of 9/8. Which of the following statements is correct?
items.explain: 9 is in the compound group (6, 9, 12). Divide 9 by 3 to get 3 beats per bar. The bottom number 8 means eighth notes, so each beat is a dotted quarter note worth three eighth notes.
options: It is simple time with 9 beats per bar, each an eighth note.
It is compound time with 3 beats per bar, each a dotted quarter note.
It is compound time with 9 beats per bar, each a dotted quarter note.
It is simple time with 3 beats per bar, each a quarter note.

items.prompt: You pick up a score and see a 4 on top of a 2 for the time signature. What type of time is this, and what note gets the beat?
items.explain: 4 is in the simple group (2, 3, 4), so this is simple time. The bottom number is 2, which stands for a half note, so each of the 4 beats is a half note. This is 4/2 time.
options: Compound time; the beat is a dotted half note.
Simple time; the beat is a quarter note.
Simple time; the beat is a half note.
Compound time; the beat is a dotted quarter note.

items.prompt: If you are listening to a piece and every beat seems to divide into three equal parts with a lilting, rolling feel, you should expect to find a compound time signature such as 6/8, 9/8, or 12/8.
items.explain: Exactly right. That triple subdivision inside the beat is the defining sound of compound time, and the numbers 6, 9, and 12 at the top of the time signature are how a composer notates it.

blocks.md: Compound time is everywhere in the music you will play. A huge amount of folk music, lullabies, and Irish jigs sit in 6/8, and you will feel that gentle, rolling "one-and-a, two-and-a" pulse the moment you try them. Barcarolles (pieces that imitate the rocking of a boat) are almost always written in 6/8 or 12/8. Even within a single piece, a composer may switch between simple and compound time to change the feel of the music entirely. Once you can spot the time signature and ask yourself "does the beat split in two or in three?", you will know straight away how the music should flow under your fingers.

- **beat division**: the way each beat is split into smaller equal parts inside a bar
- **simple time**: a time signature in which each beat divides naturally into two equal parts (for example, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4)
- **compound time**: a time signature in which each beat divides naturally into three equal parts (for example, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8)
- **compound duple**: compound time with two beats per bar (6/8)
- **compound triple**: compound time with three beats per bar (9/8)
- **compound quadruple**: compound time with four beats per bar (12/8)
- **beat note**: in compound time, the dotted note that represents one full beat (a dotted quarter note in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8)
- **grouping**: the way notes and rests are beamed or arranged within a bar to show clearly where each beat falls

- In **simple time**, every beat divides into **two** equal parts.
- In **compound time**, every beat divides into **three** equal parts.
- The most common compound time signatures are **6/8** (two beats per bar), **9/8** (three beats per bar), and **12/8** (four beats per bar).
- In these signatures the bottom number 8 means an eighth note, but the **real beat** is a **dotted quarter note** (worth three eighth notes).
- To tell simple from compound at a glance: if the top number is **2, 3 or 4**, it is simple; if it is **6, 9 or 12**, it is compound.
- Dotted notes, ties and rests follow the same rules in compound time as in simple time, but grouping must always show the **dotted-quarter beat** clearly.
- Hearing that natural "**one-and-a**" lilt is the quickest way to recognise compound time by ear.

items.prompt: In simple time, the beat divides into how many equal smaller notes?
items.explain: Simple time means each beat splits neatly into two equal parts. For example, a quarter-note beat divides into two eighth notes. Three is the answer for compound time, not simple.

items.prompt: A time signature of 6/8 is a compound time signature. What is the beat unit in 6/8, and how many of those beats are in each bar?
items.explain: In 6/8 the six eighth notes group into two groups of three. Each group of three eighth notes equals one dotted quarter note, so there are two dotted quarter-note beats per bar. The top number (6) tells you how many eighth notes there are, not how many beats.
options: Two dotted quarter-note beats per bar

items.prompt: A time signature with a top number of 9 always means there are 9 beats in every bar.
items.explain: 9/8 is a compound time signature. Its nine eighth notes group into three groups of three, giving three dotted quarter-note beats per bar, not nine. The top number counts the smallest written note units, not the felt beats.

items.prompt: In compound time, a single beat is most often written as what kind of note? (Give the note name, for example 'half note'.)
items.explain: In the most common compound time signatures (6/8, 9/8, 12/8) each beat is a dotted quarter note, which lasts three eighth notes. The dot adds half the original note's value, making it worth one and a half quarter notes, or three eighth notes.

items.prompt: You are looking at a piece of music and want to decide quickly whether it is in simple or compound time. Which of the following is the most reliable clue from the time signature alone?
items.explain: The quickest at-a-glance rule is: if the top number is 6, 9 or 12 (divisible by 3, and greater than 3), the time is almost certainly compound. The bottom number being 8 does not by itself tell you simple or compound, and not all even or large top numbers mean compound time.
options: If the top number is even, it is compound time.
If the top number is divisible by 3 (such as 6, 9 or 12), it is compound time.
If the bottom number is 8, it is always simple time.
If the top number is greater than 4, it is compound time.
